objectives: Explain why every believer should study the Bible personally
Observe a passage carefully before deciding what it means
Interpret a passage in its context and literary type
Apply Scripture to life and share it with others

modules.title: Why study the Bible?
modules.summary: What the Bible is, why it matters, and how to come to it.

lessons.title: God has spoken
lessons.body:
The Bible is not an ordinary book. "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works" (2 Timothy 3:16-17).

Because God speaks in it, the Bible does what no other book can do. It converts the soul, makes the simple wise, rejoices the heart and enlightens the eyes (Psalm 19:7-8). It is food for the soul: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4).

Listening to sermons is good, but every believer also needs to read and study for themselves. The Bereans were praised because they "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so" (Acts 17:11). Personal study protects you from error and lets God speak to you directly.

lessons.title: Coming to the Word rightly
lessons.body:
How we come to the Bible matters as much as how much we read.

- **Pray first.** "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law" (Psalm 119:18). The Holy Spirit is the true teacher (John 14:26).
- **Come humbly.** Receive "with meekness the engrafted word" (James 1:21), ready to be corrected.
- **Come to obey.** "Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only" (James 1:22).
- **Come regularly.** A set time and place helps. A little every day is better than a lot once a month.

You need only a Bible, a notebook and a pen. A good study Bible, a concordance and a Bible dictionary help, but begin with what you have. Choose one book, such as Mark or Philippians, and read it slowly over several weeks.

quiz.q: According to 2 Timothy 3:16, all scripture is:
Why were the Bereans praised in Acts 17:11?
What should we do before reading, according to Psalm 119:18?
options: Pray for God to open our eyes
Doers of the word, not hearers only

modules.title: Observation
modules.summary: Asking 'What does it say?' before 'What does it mean?'

lessons.title: Look before you leap
lessons.body:
The first step in Bible study is **observation**: noticing carefully what the passage actually says. Many mistakes come from jumping to meaning or application before reading properly. "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Proverbs 18:13).

Read the passage several times, slowly. Read it aloud. If you can, read it in two translations. Then ask the reporter's questions:

- **Who** is speaking, and to whom?
- **What** is happening or being taught?
- **Where** and **when** does it take place?
- **Why** is it said? (Look for words like *because*, *so that*, *therefore*.)
- **How** is it done?

Write your answers down. You will be surprised how much you see that you missed before.

lessons.title: Clues in the text
lessons.body:
Certain features of a passage are signposts. Train your eye to notice them:

- **Repeated words.** In Ephesians 2:1-10 notice how often *grace*, *dead* and *works* appear.
- **Commands.** What does the passage tell us to do?
- **Contrasts.** Look for *but*: "But God, who is rich in mercy..." (Ephesians 2:4) turns the whole passage.
- **Connecting words.** *Therefore* links back to what came before. Romans 12:1 ("I beseech you therefore") builds on eleven chapters of grace.
- **Lists and comparisons.** "as", "like", "so".
- **Questions** the writer asks.

Mark these in your notebook or in your Bible. Observation is like a doctor examining a patient before giving a diagnosis. The better the examination, the better the diagnosis.

quiz.q: What is the first step of Bible study?

options: Who is speaking, and to whom?

quiz.q: In Romans 12:1, the word 'therefore' shows that:
options: The verse builds on what came before
The chapter starts a new book

quiz.q: Which phrase turns Ephesians 2 from death to life?
options: But God, who is rich in mercy

modules.title: Interpretation
modules.summary: Finding what the passage meant to its first readers, and so what it means.

lessons.title: Context is king
lessons.body:
**Interpretation** asks: what did the writer mean to his first readers? A text without its context can be made to say almost anything.

Read the verses before and after. Read the whole chapter, and if possible the whole book. Ask who wrote it, to whom, and why.

For example, Jeremiah 29:11 ("I know the thoughts that I think toward you... thoughts of peace") is often quoted as a promise of quick success. But verse 10 shows it was spoken to exiles who would wait **seventy years** in Babylon. It is a promise of God's faithfulness through long hardship, which makes it even more precious.

"Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth" (2 Timothy 2:15).

lessons.title: Kinds of writing
lessons.body:
The Bible contains many kinds of writing, and each is read in its own way:

- **Narrative** (Genesis, Acts): true stories. Ask what they show about God and people; not every action described is approved.
- **Law** (Leviticus): God's covenant instructions to Israel, fulfilled in Christ.
- **Poetry** (Psalms): uses images. "The LORD is my shepherd" is picture language for real care.
- **Wisdom** (Proverbs): general truths for life, not guaranteed promises in every case.
- **Prophecy**: messages of warning and hope, often with symbols.
- **Gospels and parables**: a parable usually teaches one main point (Luke 15).
- **Letters** (Romans to Jude): teaching for churches, often answering problems.

Let Scripture interpret Scripture: unclear passages are explained by clear ones.

options: What the writer meant to the first readers
What I feel about the verse
How many times to read it

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah 29:10 show about verse 11?
options: It was spoken to exiles who would wait seventy years

quiz.q: How should Proverbs usually be read?
options: As general truths for wise living
As guaranteed promises in every case

modules.title: Application and teaching
modules.summary: Living the Word and passing it on.

lessons.title: From the page to life
lessons.body:
**Application** asks: what does this mean for me and for us today? Bible study is not finished until it changes how we think and live. Jesus compared those who hear and do His words to a wise man who built on rock (Matthew 7:24).

Useful application questions (sometimes called **SPECK**):

- Is there a **Sin** to avoid?
- Is there a **Promise** to claim (rightly understood)?
- Is there an **Example** to follow or avoid?
- Is there a **Command** to obey?
- Is there **Knowledge** about God to treasure?

Make your application specific: not "I should pray more" but "I will pray for ten minutes before work each day this week." Ezra "prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach" (Ezra 7:10).

lessons.title: Sharing what you learn
lessons.body:
What God teaches us is meant to be shared. "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another" (Colossians 3:16).

You can share by:

- Telling a friend or family member one thing you learned this week.
- Leading a simple Bible study using the three steps: observe, interpret, apply.
- Writing a short devotional for a group chat.
- Teaching children with a story and one clear point.

When you lead others, ask questions rather than lecturing: "What do you notice? What does it teach about God? What will we do?" This helps them learn to study for themselves. Paul told Timothy to pass the truth "to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2).

options: What this means for me and us today

quiz.q: In SPECK, what does C stand for?

options: I will pray for ten minutes before work each day this week

quiz.q: What did Ezra prepare his heart to do?
options: Seek, do and teach God's law

assignment.title: Practical assignment: study a passage
assignment.body:
Choose one of these passages: Psalm 1, Mark 4:35-41, or Philippians 4:4-9. Study it using the three steps of this course and hand in:

1. **Observation**: at least eight things you noticed (who, what, where, repeated words, commands, contrasts).
2. **Interpretation**: what the passage meant to its first readers, in four to six sentences, noting its context and kind of writing.
3. **Application**: two specific applications for your own life this week.
4. **Sharing**: one question you would ask a group to help them discover the main point.

Write 300 to 500 words.

final.q: What are the three steps of Bible study taught in this course?
Who is the true teacher of the Word, according to John 14:26?
Which word should alert you to a contrast?

options: A text without context can be made to say almost anything

final.q: Unclear passages should be explained by:
Jesus compared those who hear and do His words to:
options: A wise man who built on rock
A man who built on sand

final.q: What did Paul tell Timothy to do with the truth?
options: Commit it to faithful men who will teach others

final.q: Which is the best way to lead a group Bible study?
options: Ask questions that help people discover the meaning
Let one person do all the talking

final.q: What is the purpose of Bible study?
options: To know God and obey Him

reading: Howard and William Hendricks, Living By the Book
Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth
